editorial.headline: The Rental Business Behind Books, Discs and Recorded Media
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration there.
editorial.body:
KBLI 77293 concerns a particular kind of access business: renting and operational leasing, without an option to purchase, goods produced through printing and publishing. In everyday terms, it is the commercial circulation of books, magazines, comics, video games, cassettes, video discs and recordings on a rental basis. The distinction matters because the activity is framed around temporary use, not transfer of ownership. It therefore speaks to an operator maintaining a rentable catalogue of printed, published or recorded material and making it available again and again through rental or non-option operational lease arrangements. The record expressly includes rentals of video cassettes, CDs, VCDs/DVDs and similar media, placing older and newer recorded formats within the same stated activity.

Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA: it is open to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a clear national position; there is no lesser foreign stake shown in the record. It is also open at every listed business scale—Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar—rather than being described as a large-company-only activity. For a founder, that combination matters: the code is about the rental model itself, while the permitted scale range embraces the smallest listed enterprise through the largest.

Bali is the decisive exception, and it should be read without euphemism. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The Bali record marks it BLOCCATO_CLASSE_RISCHIO and states that, at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every stated scope. Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration island-wide and permanently; the cited block is tied to the moratorium of May 2026. So the national 100% ceiling remains the national ceiling, but it is not a route to PMA registration for this activity in Bali. This is not a narrower ownership cap or a condition that a foreign founder can solve by choosing a different participation level: it is a Bali PMA-registration block founded on the stated risk-class moratorium. The responsible reading is simple: national openness describes the code’s position in Indonesia, while Bali’s current status prevents PMA registration there.
